sections.authorBiography: Sophocles (about 497/6 to 406/5 B.C.E.) was one of the three great tragic poets of Athens, with Aeschylus and Euripides. He was born at Colonus, just outside the city, served Athens as a general and a treasurer, and is said to have written more than 120 plays, of which seven survive complete. He won first prize at the City Dionysia many times and is credited with adding a third actor to the stage.

publicationAndReception.now: Modern readers still argue over it: Hegel read it as a clash of two rightful powers, while Jebb held that the right is wholly with Antigone; in 1845 it was staged in London with Mendelssohn's music (Jebb, 1891, Introduction, § 18).

sections.laterInfluence: Later critics have kept arguing over the play: Hegel read it as a collision of two powers, family and the gods below against the State (Hegel, 1838/1920), while Jebb held that the right is wholly with Antigone (Jebb, 1891, Introduction, § 7). Goethe wished the brother argument (lines 849–854) could be removed (Eckermann, 1850, 28 March 1827). Mendelssohn wrote music for a German Antigone in 1841, and that production was staged at Covent Garden in London on 2 January 1845 (Jebb, 1891, Introduction, § 18). The play is still taught as a debate between law and conscience.
sections.overview: After the brothers Eteocles and Polyneices kill each other in a war for Thebes, their uncle Creon, the new king, forbids anyone to bury Polyneices. Their sister Antigone decides to bury him anyway, and must face the king's law.

segments.script: Say: Before we start, I want to tell you about some hard parts of this play. It is an ancient Greek tragedy about a young woman who defies a king's order so that she can honor her dead brother. The play includes war and violence within a family, references to incest in the family's past, threats of execution, self-harm, and several deaths, including deaths by suicide. These events happen offstage and are reported by others, and Sophocles shows them as a catastrophe, not as brave or as a solution. In real life, hurting yourself is wrong and is never the answer. If you or someone you know is struggling or thinking about suicide or self-harm, call or text 988, or chat at 988lifeline.org (the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline), or talk to a school counselor or a trusted adult. You don't have to handle it alone. Before we open Antigone: which matters more, divine law and human law or family and the State? Write for five minutes.

segments.phase: I do: the book in one passage
segments.activity: Model a close reading of one passage using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Ismene, sister of my blood and heart, / See’st thou how Zeus would in our lives fulfil / The weird of Oedipus, a world of woes” slowly and put it in my own words: In these lines Antigone speaks at a turning point of the section, which is about two sisters, one choice. Next, craft. I notice how the lines use characterization, conflict to make the audience feel the pressure of the moment on Antigone. The strongest word is “Oedipus”: the word “Oedipus” carries the weight of the lines and points to the section's big idea. Then, effect. What do lines 1–3 reveal about two sisters, one choice? My answer: The sisters embody two answers to an unjust law: open defiance and fearful obedience. Ismene's "weak women" (line 60) states her society's view of women, which Antigone's action challenges. These lines show two sisters, one choice, and that matters for what follows in the play.

segments.activity: Exit ticket on the author and context (answer given).
segments.script: Sophocles wrote Antigone for an Athens led by Pericles, a democracy proud of its laws. strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this scene, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in Antigone.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about Antigone: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

segments.activity: Students write to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Project the day's bell-ringer question (each lesson of Antigone has its own). Students write silently for 5 minutes, then pair-share for 3. Call on one volunteer and one non-volunteer, and connect their answers to divine law and human law.

segments.activity: The day's key words in context, with verified word histories.
segments.script: Introduce the day's words in the sentences where they appear in Antigone. Read each sentence aloud, ask students to guess the meaning from context, then give the gloss and the word history. Students copy one word into their journal with their own sentence.

Give the 10-minute background talk from the day's lesson: what happens in this scene, the context a reader needs, and the literary elements to watch. Pause once to ask a check-for-understanding question.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud in the day's lesson.
segments.script: Read the anchor passage aloud twice. Model the three steps out loud: what the words say, what craft choice stands out and why, and what effect it has on the reader. The day's lesson gives the passage and a full written think-aloud.

segments.activity: Guided analysis of a second quotation; expected answers given.
segments.script: Display the second passage. Students annotate it in pairs using the same three steps; circulate, then take answers to the two guided questions and confirm them against the expected answers in the day's lesson.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Students annotate the scene on their own (three marks with a margin note each) and write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph on the day's focus, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions, with facilitation notes.
segments.script: Run a 10-minute discussion from the day's anchor question and tiered questions. Start with literal checks, move to inference, and end with one evaluative question that ties the scene to divine law and human law.

segments.activity: Scene quiz in the app and an exit ticket (answer given).
segments.script: Students take the scene quiz in the app, then answer the one-sentence exit ticket with a short quotation. Collect the tickets to plan the next lesson.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Restate the day's takeaway in one sentence, ask two students to name the line that best proves it, and preview the next reading in Antigone.

finalPaper.exemplar: The sisters embody two answers to an unjust law: open defiance and fearful obedience. Ismene's "weak women" (line 60) states her society's view of women, which Antigone's action challenges. The text makes this visible when it says “If in defiance of the law we cross / A monarch’s will?—weak women, think of that, / Not framed by nature to contend with men” (Prologue, lines 59–61). Before dawn after the war, Antigone tells her sister Ismene that King Creon has forbidden anyone to bury their brother Polyneices, who attacked Thebes; Eteocles, who defended it, will be buried with honour. Antigone will bury Polyneices and asks Ismene to help. Ismene, recalling the ruin of their family, refuses: they are women and cannot defy the State. Antigone goes alone. A full paper would carry this reading through the beginning, middle and end, and answer the strongest competing reading.
